Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
619 PM EST Wed Nov 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 237 PM EST Wednesday...

A Wind Advisory and a Winter Weather Advisory have been issued for 
the Thanksgiving evening and overnight hours for portions of the 
region.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 237 PM EST Wednesday...

1. Pockets of freezing rain across northern New York and 
central and northeastern Vermont may cause slippery travel Thanksgiving
evening and overnight. 

2. Isolated to scattered power outages near the western slopes 
of the central and southern Greens are possible associated with 
strong east winds. 

3. Next chance for precipitation will come Sunday night into 
Monday as a frontal system crosses our region.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 237 PM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A potent and large low pressure system will track 
northward from interior North Carolina into western Pennsylvania on 
Thanksgiving Day. We are dodging a bullet with regards to this storm 
track, which could have resulted in more widespread and greater 
amounts of freezing rain; because high pressure will be retreating 
there will be only marginally cold air to support wintry weather. 
Given holiday travel, caution will be advised for slippery spots 
given lack of treatment in this early season. While a Winter Weather 
Advisory has been issued from tomorrow at 4 PM through Friday at 7 
AM, we think the impacts for this event will be on the lower side. 

One mitigating factor against more widespread impact are expected 
road temperatures primarily in the middle 30s, consistent with 
recent warmth and sunshine along with air temperatures barely 
falling below freezing in areas that see ice accumulations. Also, 
forecast soundings show the wedge of sub-freezing air will be too 
shallow for any other precipitation type besides freezing rain (no 
risk of sleet/snow), and the depth of this layer favors ice 
accretion primarily above 1500 feet in most areas. Strong easterly 
winds near the surface overnight, which are discussed in Key Message 
2, also should lead to eventual erosion of this sub-freezing layer 
in areas along and west of higher terrain. In contrast, areas upwind 
such as near Route 100 in central Vermont will see more persistent 
cold air result in a more likely ice accumulation. In northern New 
York, stronger northeasterly flow in the St. Lawrence Valley will 
also support a greater chance of sub-freezing temperatures being 
more persistent and accordingly, some ice accretion on untreated 
surfaces. Conditions should improve by Friday morning due to 
combination of steady rain ending and continued warming.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Strong easterly winds continue to be of some concern, 
particularly in areas immediately downslope of the Green Mountains 
in central and southern Vermont where a Wind Advisory is now in 
effect. The timeframe of strongest winds is tricky, but there is 
very good consensus that the low level jet will become situated 
below inversion height and high resolution guidance shows a 
localized, favorably sharp west-east pressure gradient developing in 
pressure fields towards 10 PM, concurrent with a 70 knot east-
southeast wind field in the 875 to 925 millibar layer just above a 
shallow low level inversion. Cross sections show some mountain wave 
breaking, which would be expected to extend only a short distance 
from our mountain peaks. Therefore, the potential for damaging winds 
currently looks isolated to the more immediate western slopes. This 
threat of localized 55 MPH gusts is favored towards our southern 
areas; the orientation of the spine of the Greens relative to wind 
direction north of Camel's Hump, along with a weakening jet, 
makes the threat lower farther north. The strongest winds are 
also favored after steady rain ends, which opens up mainly a 1 
to 3 hour window for the most notable impacts spreading 
northward after midnight.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Sunday night into Monday will bring our next chance for 
any weather as a low pressure system and associated fronts will 
cross our forecast area. Minimal impacts are expected with this 
system as boundary layer temperatures will be mild enough that 
precipitation type will be mainly light rain/rain showers in all but 
the highest elevations. There could be a change over to show showers 
as the precipitation comes to an end Monday night, especially across 
the northern higher elevation areas. After maximum temperatures on 
Monday reach the mid 40s to around 50 in the afternoon, cold air 
rushes in behind departing system and lows will dip back into the 
20s.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z THURSDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 00Z Friday...VFR with high clouds bkn-ovc200-250 and
light variable winds except SE 5-7kts at KRUT through 12z
Thursday. Clouds continue to thicken and lower but remain VFR
through the period. Light winds <5 kts will gradually increase
to ESE at 10-15 kts and gusty at KRUT after 15z and ENE at KMSS
13-18kts. LLWS will develop across southern VT shortly after 18z
and lift northward especially after 00z Fri along with 
increasing at the SFC.

Rain enters VT/MA border around 20-21z, lifting to KRUT ard/aft
22z and elsewhere after 00z Fri.
